'''''Physalis peruviana''''' is a South American species of plant in the nightshade family ([[Solanaceae]]). Within its native range, it is called '''aguaymanto''', '''uvilla''' or '''uchuva''', in addition to numerous indigenous and regional names. In English, its common names include '''Cape gooseberry''', '''goldenberry''' and '''Peruvian groundcherry'''.{{r|morton|cabi|lostcrops}}<ref name="ITIS">{{ITIS |id=30587 |taxon=''Physalis'' |access-date=2011-05-21}}</ref>

The history of ''P. peruviana'' cultivation in South America can be traced to the [[Inca Empire]]. It has been cultivated in England since the late 18th century, and in [[South Africa]] since at least the start of the 19th century. Widely introduced in the 20th century, it is now cultivated or grows wild across the world in temperate and tropical regions.

== Description ==
''P. peruviana'' is an [[annual plant|annual]] in temperate locations, but a [[perennial]] in the tropics.<ref name="morton" /> As a perennial, it develops into a diffusely branched shrub reaching {{convert|1-1.6|m|ft|abbr=off|frac=2}} in height, with spreading branches and velvety, heart-shaped [[leaves]].<ref name="cabi" /> The [[hermaphrodite]] flowers are bell-shaped and drooping, {{Convert|15-20|mm|abbr=off|frac=8}} across, and yellow with purple-brown internal spots. After the flower falls, the [[Sepal|calyx]] expands, ultimately forming a beige husk fully enclosing the fruit.<ref name="morton" /><ref name="cabi" />

The inflated, papery calyx is a prominent feature. The calyx is [[wikt:accrescent|accrescent]] until the fruit is fully grown; at first, it is of normal size, but after the petals fall, it continues to grow until it forms a protective cover around the growing fruit. If the fruit is left inside the intact calyx husks, its shelf life at room temperature is about 30–45 days. The calyx is inedible.

The fruit is a round, smooth [[berry (botany)|berry]], resembling a miniature yellow tomato {{Convert|1.25-2|cm|frac=4}} wide.<ref name="cabi" /> Removed from its calyx, it is bright yellow to orange in color, and sweet when ripe, with a characteristic, mildly tart grape-like flavor.<ref name="morton" />

== Taxonomy ==
''P. peruviana'' is closely related to the [[tomatillo]].<ref name="morton" /> As a member of the plant family [[Solanaceae]], it is also more distantly related to a large number of edible plants, including [[tomato]]es, [[eggplant]]s, and [[potato]]es.<ref name="morton" />

''Physalis peruviana'' was given a botanical [[species description]] by [[Carl Linnaeus]] in 1763.{{r|ipni}} and given the genus name ''Physalis'' after the [[Greek language|Greek]] φυσαλλίς (''physallís'', 'bladder, wind instrument') in reference to the calyx that surrounds the berry. The specific name ''peruviana'' refer to the country of [[Peru]], one of the countries of the berry's origin.

It was grown in England in 1774 and by early settlers of South Africa's [[Cape of Good Hope]] before 1807.<ref name="morton" /> Whether it was grown there before its introduction to England is not known, but sources since the mid-19th century attribute the common English name "Cape gooseberry" to this fact.{{r|vonm1884|loudon1842}} An alternative suggestion is that name refers to the calyx surrounding the fruit like a [[cape]], possibly an example of [[false etymology]], because it does not appear in publications earlier than the mid-20th century. Not long after its introduction to South Africa, ''P. peruviana'' was introduced to Australia, New Zealand and various [[Pacific islands]].<ref name="morton" /> Despite its common name, it is not botanically related to the true gooseberries of the genus ''[[Ribes]]''.

In Peru, ''P. peruviana'' is known as {{lang|es|aguaymanto}} in Spanish and {{lang|qu|topotopo}} in [[Quechuan languages|Quechua]].<ref>{{Cite web|title=Discover the aguaymanto, one of the best foods produced in Peru|url=https://peru.info/en-us/gastronomy/news/2/12/discover-the-aguaymanto--one-of-the-best-foods-produced-in-peru|access-date=2020-07-29|website=peru.info|language=en-US}}</ref> In neighboring Colombia, it is known by its [[Aymaran language|Aymara]] name as {{lang|es|uchuva}},<ref>{{Cite web|title=Uchuvas|url=https://www.flavorsofbogota.com/uchuvas/|access-date=2020-08-09|website=flavorsofbogota.com|date=30 May 2019 |language=en-US}}</ref> and as ''uvilla'' (Spanish for 'little grape') in [[Ecuador]].<ref name="visitecuador">{{Cite web |last=Carpio |first=Cristina Pettersen |date=2021-07-10 |title=Ecuadorian fruit: uvilla - Ecuador |url=https://visitecuadorandsouthamerica.com/en/ecuadorian-fruit-uvilla/ |access-date=2023-02-25 |website=Visit Ecuador and South America |language=en-US}}</ref>

==Distribution and habitat==
The species is reportedly native to [[Chile]] and [[Peru]].<ref name="morton" /> Its center of genetic diversity is in the [[Andes Mountains]] of Ecuador, [[Chile]], [[Colombia]], and Peru.{{Citation needed|date=August 2026}} It grows in forests, forest edges, and [[riparian]] areas.<ref name="cabi" /> It grows at high elevations of {{convert|500–3000|m|abbr=on}} in its native region, but may also be found at [[sea level]] in [[Oceania]] and Pacific islands where it occurs widely in subtropical and warm, temperate conditions.<ref name="cabi" /> Its [[latitude]] range is about 45°S to 60°N, and its altitude range is generally from [[sea level]] to {{convert|3000|m|abbr=on}}.<ref name="cabi" /> The plant has become [[invasive species|invasive]] in some natural habitats, forming [[thicket]]s, particularly in [[Hawaii]] and on other Pacific islands.<ref name="cabi" /> There are believed to be dozens of [[ecotype]]s worldwide that differentiated by plant size, calyx shape, and the size, color, and flavor of the fruit. Wild forms are thought to be diploid with 2''n'' = 24 [[chromosome]]s, while cultivated forms include varieties with increased [[ploidy]] and 32 or 48 chromosomes.<ref name="garcia-godos">{{Cite journal |last1=García-Godos Alcázar |first1=Paula |last2=Palomino Felices |first2=Sonia |last3=Martínez Gómez |first3=Keny |date=2020-01-01 |title=Diversidad citogenética de ''Physalis peruviana'' L. 'aguaymanto' de los ecotipos del Perú |language=es |journal=Investigación |volume=28 |issue=1 |pages=157–165 |doi=10.51440/unsch.revistainvestigacion.28.1.2020.368 |issn=2709-8583|doi-access=free }}</ref>

==Cultivation==
The history of ''P. peruviana'' cultivation in South America can be traced to the [[Inca Empire]].<ref>(Cailes 1952; Legge 1974a)</ref><ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=j8IKr-EPDzoC&pg=PA425|title=New Zealand Journal of Agricultural Research|date=1986|publisher=The [[Royal Society of New Zealand]]|pages=425|language=en}}</ref>

It has been widely introduced into cultivation in tropical, subtropical, and temperate areas such as Australia, China, India, Malaysia, and the Philippines.<ref name="morton" /><ref name="cabi" /><ref>{{Cite web |url=http://cc2.savs.hcc.edu.tw/~chuavv/Philippines/PhilippineFruits/index.html |title=Fr. Visminlu Vicente L. Chua, S.J., ''Philippine Fruits''. Published online: 1 September 2015. |access-date=6 December 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180416082814/http://cc2.savs.hcc.edu.tw/~chuavv/Philippines/PhilippineFruits/index.html |archive-date=16 April 2018 |url-status=dead }}</ref> ''P. peruviana'' thrives at an annual average temperature from {{convert|13|to|18|C|F}}, tolerating temperatures as high as {{convert|30|C|F}}.<ref name="cabi" /> It grows well in [[Mediterranean climate|Mediterranean]] climates and is hardy to [[USDA hardiness zone]] 8, meaning it can be damaged by [[frost]].<ref name="cabi" /> It grows well in annual rainfalls of {{convert|800|–|4300|mm|in|abbr=on}} if the soil is well drained, prefers full sun or partial shade in well-drained soil, and grows vigorously in sandy [[loam]].<ref name="morton" /><ref name="cabi" />

The plant is readily grown from seeds, which are abundant (100 to 300 per fruit), but with low [[germination]] rates, requiring thousands of seeds to sow a [[hectare]].<ref name="morton" /> Plants grown from year-old stem cuttings will flower early and yield well, but are less vigorous than those grown from seed.<ref name="morton" />

===Pests and diseases===
In South Africa, [[cutworm]]s attack the Cape gooseberry in seedbeds, [[red spider]] mites in the field, and [[potato tuber moth]]s near potato fields. [[Hares]] damage young plants, and birds eat the fruits. [[Mite]]s, [[whiteflies]] and [[flea beetle]]s can also be problematic.<ref name="morton" /> [[Powdery mildew]], [[Coccus hesperidum|soft brown scale]], [[root rot]] and viruses may affect plants.<ref name="morton" /> In [[New Zealand]], plants can be infected by ''[[Candidatus]]'' ''Liberibacter solanacearum''.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Liefting |first=L. W. |author2=L. I. Ward |author3=J. B. Shiller |author4=G. R. G. Clover  |year=2008 |title=A new <nowiki>'</nowiki>''Candidatus'' Liberibacter<nowiki>'</nowiki> species in ''Solanum betaceum'' (Tamarillo) and ''Physalis peruviana'' (Cape gooseberry) in New Zealand |journal=Plant Disease |volume=92 |issue=11 |pages=1588 |doi=10.1094/PDIS-92-11-1588B |pmid=30764458 |doi-access=free }}</ref>

== Potential toxicity ==
Unripe raw fruits, flowers, leaves, and stems of the plant contain [[solanine]] and [[solanidine]] [[alkaloid]]s that may cause poisoning if ingested by humans, [[cattle]] or horses.<ref name="ncsu">{{cite web |title=Physalis |url=https://plants.ces.ncsu.edu/plants/physalis/ |publisher=North Carolina State University, Extension Gardener |access-date=23 February 2023 |date=2023}}</ref><ref name="csu">{{cite web |title=Ground cherry, Chinese lantern |url=https://csuvth.colostate.edu/poisonous_plants/Plants/Details/93 |publisher=Guide to Poisonous Plants, Colorado State University |access-date=23 February 2023 |date=2022}}</ref>

===Nutrition===
Raw Cape gooseberries are 85% water, 11% [[carbohydrate]]s, 2% [[protein (nutrient)|protein]], and 1% [[fat]]. In a reference amount of {{convert|100|g}}, raw Cape gooseberries supply 53 [[calorie]]s and provide moderate levels (10–19% of the [[Daily Value]]) of [[Vitamin B3|niacin]] and [[vitamin C]].

Analyses of [[oil]] from different berry components, primarily its seeds, showed that [[linoleic acid]] and [[oleic acid]] were the main [[fatty acids]], [[beta-sitosterol]] and [[campesterol]] were principal [[phytosterol]]s, and the oil contained [[vitamin K]] and [[beta-carotene]].<ref>{{cite journal|journal=Journal of Agricultural and Food Chemistry|year=2003|volume=51|issue=4|pages=969–74|title=Oil goldenberry (''Physalis peruviana'' L.)|vauthors=Ramadan MF, Mörsel JT |pmid=12568557|doi=10.1021/jf020778z}}</ref>

===Culinary===
''P. peruviana'' is an economically useful crop as an exotic exported fruit, and is favored in breeding and cultivation programs of many countries.<ref name=cabi/> ''P. peruviana'' fruits are marketed in the United States as ''goldenberry'' and sometimes ''Pichuberry'', named after [[Machu Picchu]] in order to associate the fruit with its cultivation in Peru.<ref>{{cite news|last=Galarza|first=Daniella|title=This Goose(berry) is Cooked: Let's Talk About the Pichuberry|url=http://www.lamag.com/lafood/digestblog/2013/06/18/this-gooseberry-is-cooked-lets-talk-about-the-pichuberry|newspaper=Los Angeles Magazine|access-date=19 April 2014|date=2013-06-18}}</ref>

Cape gooseberries are made into fruit-based sauces, pies, [[pudding]]s, [[chutney]]s, jams and ice cream, or eaten fresh in salads and fruit salads.<ref name=morton/> In [[Latin America]], it is often consumed as a ''batido'' or [[smoothie]],<ref>{{Cite web|title=Five amazing natural juices with Colombian fruit and vegetables|url=https://www.colombia.co/en/colombia-culture/five-amazing-natural-juice-recipes-with-colombian-fruit-and-vegetables/|access-date=2020-08-09|website=colombia.co|date=29 May 2019 |language=en-US}}</ref> and because of its showy husk, it is used in restaurants as a decorative garnish for [[dessert]]s. To enhance its food uses, hot air drying improves qualities of [[dietary fiber]] content, texture and appearance.<ref>{{cite journal|pmc=4375184|year=2013|last1=Vega-Gálvez|first1=A|title=Influence of drying temperature on dietary fibre, rehydration properties, texture and microstructure of Cape gooseberry (''Physalis peruviana'' L.)|journal=Journal of Food Science and Technology|volume=52|issue=4|pages=2304–2311|last2=Zura-Bravo|first2=L|last3=Lemus-Mondaca|first3=R|last4=Martinez-Monzó|first4=J|last5=Quispe-Fuentes|first5=I|last6=Puente|first6=L|last7=Di Scala|first7=K|doi=10.1007/s13197-013-1235-0|pmid=25829613}}</ref>

In [[basic research]] on fruit maturation, the content of [[polyphenol]]s and vitamin C varied by [[cultivar]], harvest time, and ripening stage.<ref>{{cite journal|pmid=25131258|year=2015|last1=Bravo|first1=K|title=Influence of cultivar and ripening time on bioactive compounds and antioxidant properties in Cape gooseberry (''Physalis peruviana'' L.)|journal=Journal of the Science of Food and Agriculture|volume=95|issue=7|pages=1562–9|last2=Sepulveda-Ortega|first2=S|last3=Lara-Guzman|first3=O|last4=Navas-Arboleda|first4=A. A.|last5=Osorio|first5=E|doi=10.1002/jsfa.6866|doi-access=free}}</ref>
